newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.

text.p: KEMP SAYS LABOR'S WORK FOR THE DOLE BACKDOWN HUMILIATING
The Federal Government says its Work for the Dole projects will be up and running by October, now that the Opposition has given its support.
The Training Minister, David Kemp, says the Government will invite submissions on possible projects to be funded in areas with high rates of youth unemployment.
Doctor Kemp says the Government will provide 10,000 places in the first year.
He says Labor's decision to support the scheme is one of the most humiliating backflips he has ever seen.
The Minister says Opposition Leader Kim Beazley should be exhausted after the "acrobatics" of the past 24 hours.
ACTING PM SAYS PROSSER HAS HIS SUPPORT
Acting Prime Minister Tim Fischer has told Coalition MP's he will continue to support Small Business Minister Geoff Prosser.
Mr Prosser is under increasing pressure from the Opposition to resign, after acknowledging he had raised personal business interests in a phone call to Coles-Myer Chairman, Nick Greiner.
Mr Prosser has told Parliament, he discussed with Mr Greiner the possibility of a Target store opening at his Eaton shopping centre in Western Australia.
Opposition Leader Kim Beazley says Mr Prosser has breached every section of the Prime Minister's code of conduct, and must go.
But Mr Fischer has told a joint Coalition parties meeting in Canberra, Mr Prosser will continue to have his support.
TELSTRA TO RECOMMEND EMPLOYEES KEEP MATERNITY LEAVE
Telstra says it will recommend its majority owned subsidiary Pacific Access maintain maternity leave for workers moving to the company.
Pacific Access, 62.5 per cent owned by Telstra, last week won the contract to produce Telstra's White Pages.
The Public Sector Union says the 650 employees, a majority of whom are women, who will transfer from Telstra to the new company, stand to lose their right to twelve weeks paid maternity leave.
The Federal Government says it's a commercial matter.
Telstra spokeswoman Karen Halfpenny has told Radio National, Telstra would recommend to Pacific Access that the paid maternity leave be maintained.
Ms Halfpenny says recommendations are being put to the Pacific Access board, to ensure that those Telstra employees who resign and take up an offer with Pacific Access, don't lose their conditions.
COUNCIL BEGINS LOOKING AT ETHICS OF GENE TECHNOLOGY

The National Health and Medical Research Council has begun probing new areas of the ethics associated with gene technology. The Council, which has been appointed for the next three years, is in Hobart for its first meeting.
The youngest member, 21-year-old Celia Kemp from Melbourne, says advances in gene technology are testing conventional attitudes.
Ms Kemp says gene technology is an ethical minefield, which many people feel strongly about.
She says on issues such as patenting genes, the Council is considering putting up some structures and proposals, and perhaps releasing a report in the future.
SEARCH FOR TODDLER CONTINUING NEAR MOE
In Victoria, the father of missing Moe toddler, Jaidyn Leskie, has been briefed by police about today's seachers around the Gippsland city.
Rain at Moe is reducing visibility.
Some 140 police and volunteers have so far been unable to turn up any evidence that may lead to the whereabouts of the 14-month old toddler.
His father Brett Leskie was visibly upset when he visited the Edward Hunter Reserve this afternoon.
Mr Leskie has praised Police for their efforts, but says the thought that Jaidyn could be in the swamp makes him sick to the stomach.
ICI FOUND NEGLIGENT IN BIGGEST CLASS ACTION BY PRIMARY PRODUCERS
Chemical giant ICI has been found negligent following a beef contamination scare involving hundreds of farmers from two states.
Hailed as the biggest class action by primary producers, 480 cattle producers from New South Wales and Queensland sued ICI over the manufacture and distribution of the chemical, Helix.
Chemical residue was found in their cattle when during a drought, the livestock were fed cotton trash which had been sprayed with Helix.
It led to a beef contamination scare and a temporary freeze on some exports.
The Federal Court ruled ICI breached its duty of care in four separate categories.
But the Court dismissed negligent claims against the New South Wales and Queensland Governments.
A separate trial will determine damages.
GOVT CONSIDERS CHANGE TO LAW OVER FAMILY COURT MATTERS
The Federal Government is considering relaxing laws which ban the publication of family court matters.
A report to the Attorney General, Daryl Williams, recommends publication of all cases, including the names of parties, except in sensitive circumstances or when it concerns parental arrangements.
The report by the former Chief Judge of the West Australian Family Court, Ian McCall, says there are compelling reasons to relax media restrictions on family court cases.
Mr Williams says one reason for the recommendation is the issue of public confidence in the Court, and the need for justice to be seen to be done.
The Attorney General says he has asked his department to seek community views on the recommendations, with a view to changing legislation.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
